newsitem.title: UK: British mutuals pay to compete with banks.
newsitem.headline: British mutuals pay to compete with banks.

text.p: Britain's mutually-owned building societies returned some 400 million stg to their customers in 1996 in the form of higher savings rates and lower borrowing rates than banks, the Building Societies Commission said on Monday.

The BSC said its survey showed that continuing building societies (those not converting to bank status and floating on the stock exchange) cut the gap between their retail mortgage rates and their savings rates by 58 basis points from 2.08 percent to 1.50 percent.
The BSC said the figures showed that building societies could continue to provide strong competition to banks in the mortgage and liquid savings markets.

Many societies, such as the Nationwide, have adopted a policy of returning profits to members via more competitive rates in order to fend off pressure for conversion and the share windfall that this brings.
The BSC noted that the transfer of money to members has not meant that that the capital solvency ratios of the building societies have suffered.
They stand at an average 13.5 percent compared to the EU minimum standard of eight percent.

With their lower cost base and because they do not have to pay dividends, the BSC said the building societies should be able to manage with a lower net interest margin and lower profit levels than banks offering similar products.
